source.title: Individual Parameters in Weight-Sparse Transformers Appear Interpretable

record.tranche_reason: The study measures interpretability of individual weights, not neuron poles or neuron explanations as specified by the claim versions. Its neuron case study gives related evidence, but does not test any listed version.
record.gate_note: The headline percentages (including 15.0% for Gao et al. and 9.6% for Drori sparse) concern sampled nonzero weights, so they are not rows for neuron-pole claims. The neuron 2461 case study reports activation-level behavior and a weight-level decomposition; these are recorded as related findings under versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The study scores explanations of individual nonzero weights by ablation on held-out text in small weight-sparse and dense transformers. It does not audit neuron poles, does not score neuron explanations by activation simulation, and does not examine InceptionV1 or attribution graphs. Its neuron case studies (digit neuron, quote neurons, speech-verb neuron 2461) decompose neurons into input-weight roles, which is a related construct, not a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that a substantial fraction of nonzero weights in weight-sparse transformers have held-out-verified explanations of when they matter, versus nearly none in dense models. The cross-model ordering is robust to threshold, candidate budget and LLM. Higher-impact weights are more interpretable. The pipeline explains when a weight matters, not what it computes, and the reported rates are a lower bound.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses single-weight ablation, LLM-generated token-context predicates, and conditional-zero scoring on held-out text; it does not use neuron-pole audits or neuron activation explanations.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported rates vary with the auto-interp LLM and candidate budget; the cross-model ordering is preserved in the tested sweeps. For the string-closing example, the score changes from -0.98 with token-local predicates to +0.83 when look-back is allowed.

fits_no_version.finding: In the Drori-sparse model, neuron 2461 reads at activation level as a speech-verb detector. Its top 20 input weights split into five role groups: activators, mental-verb and modal suppressors, punctuation gates and specific-token gates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A neuron with a coherent activation-level label can be composed of several distinct weight-level gating roles.

fits_no_version.finding: Robust per-weight interpretability rates are 15.0% (Gao sparse), 9.6% (Drori sparse), 1.5% (Drori dense) and 0.4% (Pythia-70m). The sparse–dense gap widens under held-out resampling, and stronger auto-interp LLMs give higher rates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual nonzero weights are far more often interpretable in weight-sparse transformers than in dense ones, and measured rates depend on explainer strength.

record.problems: The measurements concern weights rather than neuron poles, so they cannot establish the claimed neuron-level percentages. The neuron case study is a single neuron; only 20 of its 86 nonzero input weights were profiled, with 66 excluded as below the metric's noise floor. The authors also note that their predicate language cannot express some semantic or stateful features and that distribution-shift robustness is out of scope.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows. The paper's aggregate interpretability rates and ablations concern individual weights and were excluded because they do not measure neuron-pole interpretability.

untested.parts: No neuron-pole audit and no Qwen3-32B; no shares of one-job, two-job or unexplained poles.
Four small models are compared on per-weight interpretability, not neuron-pole shares; no MoE or large-scale models.
No vision models, no cat-and-car neuron, no recursive generalization analysis.
Sparse versus dense per-weight rates and the LLM-strength effect concern weights, not neuron interpretability shares; no vision estimates.
No attribution graphs or replacement-model comparison.
Neuron explanations from activating examples are not tested for predicting firing. Weight predicates are tested on held-out text instead.
No simulation scoring of neuron activations. Weight-level rates rise with stronger LLMs (up to ~30 points), but these are weights, not neurons.

missing.what: Aggregate per-weight rates are not recorded (Table 1: InterpA, InterpB and robust rates for four models). They bear on no version but would be useful under fits_no_version.
Digit-detection neuron 1863 (nine input weights, each separately interpretable, grouped into digit-count gates) and quote-detector neurons 863 and 2790 are not recorded.
missing.locator: Section 5; Appendix A.6, A.7; Figure 7, Figure 17; Table 3

record.verdict_notes: The reader's relation (discusses) and tranche (T6) are appropriate. The paper's unit is the weight, not the neuron. The neuron case studies are single illustrative examples with no population estimate. I set both rows to cannot_determine because no version is linked.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not audit neuron poles or estimate the shares with one job, two related jobs, or not-yet-understood jobs.
The study compares four models, but measures per-weight interpretability, not neuron-pole shares; it does not test dense and MoE models up to trillions of parameters.
It does not examine InceptionV1's cat-and-car neuron or recursive generalization.
It compares sparse and dense language models, but does not test the essay's claims about architecture, regularization, vision models, or the estimated 5% to 99% range.
It does not build attribution graphs or test whether neuron-based graphs explain behavior without a replacement model.
It tests weight predicates on held-out text, not neuron explanations derived from activating examples or their ability to predict neuron firing.
It scores weight-level explanations, not neuron explanations scored by simulating neuron activations on new text.

rows.subject: Drori (2026), sparse, layer-1 MLP pre-GELU neuron 2461
rows.operation_detail: Inspected pre-GELU activation contexts on the SimpleStories corpus, sampling contexts from the top-95% activation bands.

conditions.value: top-95%; five context snippets per direction

rows.measure: Activation-level positive and negative context patterns
rows.value: Positive activations were concentrated on speech verbs; negative activations were dominated by the copulas is and are. The authors describe the neuron at activation level as a speech-verb detector.
rows.note: This is one neuron case study, not a population estimate of neuron interpretability or pole-level job counts.
rows.check: A qualitative activation-level description of a single neuron with no population share or explanation score, so it can't show any version's effect. 'observed' has no version to be observed against.

source_check.problem: none; single-neuron qualitative description, cannot_determine fits

rows.subject: Drori (2026), sparse, layer-1 MLP pre-GELU neuron 2461
rows.operation_detail: Profiled the top 20 of the neuron's 86 nonzero input weights by max-KL and assigned roles from per-weight predicates.
rows.measure: Weight-level functional-role groups within the neuron
rows.value: Five clusters were reported: speech-verb activators (six channels), mental-verb suppressors (three), a modal-verb suppressor (one), punctuation gates (seven), and specific-token gates (three). The remaining 66 weights were not analyzed because their ablation effects were below the metric's noise floor on this corpus.
rows.note: The study says the single activation-level label conceals multiple weight-level roles. This does not estimate how often neurons have one or multiple main jobs.
rows.check: A weight-level role decomposition of one neuron (20 of 86 weights profiled). It measures input-weight roles, not neuron poles, jobs or activation-prediction scores.

relation.reason: The appendix contrasts the neuron-level autointerp label with the weight-level view for one neuron. That is a discussion, not a test of any version.

tranche.reason: The study scores individual weights by ablation. It audits no neuron poles and scores no neuron explanations by simulation. The single-neuron case is illustrative only.

source_check.notes: Both rows are from one neuron in one sparse model. The study offers a single-neuron illustration that an activation-level label can hide several weight-level roles. It gives no population estimate, so it bears on no version.
